title: Applied (AMAT) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
transcript:
Clean room capacity now gates how fast chip equipment can scale.

DATE

Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

TAKEAWAYS

RISKS

SUMMARY

Applied Materials, Inc.(AMAT-3.58%)reported record financial results for the fourth quarter and fiscal year 2026, noting that performance was driven by demand for artificial intelligence computing across foundry-logic, DRAM, and advanced packaging segments. Management reported that the company is outgrowing the wafer fab equipment market due to leadership positions in enabling technologies for the artificial intelligence era. The company stated that it has gained significant customer visibility, with major clients providing rolling eight-quarter demand forecasts to align on capacity ramp expectations. Applied Materials is investing in manufacturing and lab capacity to support projected long-term growth in semiconductor demand while focusing on increasing operating leverage through internal AI adoption and support function automation.

INDUSTRY GLOSSARY

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator:Welcome to the Applied Materials Fourth Quarter of Fiscal 2026 Earnings Call.[Operator Instructions]I would now like to turn the call over to Mike Sullivan, Corporate Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Michael Sullivan:Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining today's call. With me are Gary Dickerson, our President and CEO; and Brice Hill, our Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that today's call includes forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ. Information concerning these risks and uncertainties is discussed in our most recent Form 10-Q and other filings with the SEC. Today's call also includes non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliations to GAAP measures can be found in today's earnings press release and in our quarterly earnings materials, which are available on our website at ir.appliedmaterials.com.

In addition, any comments regarding calendar 2026 refer to fiscal Q2 2026 through fiscal Q1 2027. And with that introduction, I'd now like to turn the call over to Gary Dickerson.

Gary Dickerson:Thanks, Mike. With quarterly results at the top end of our guidance range and all-time highs for revenue and profitability, Applied delivered a record fiscal 2026 and our seventh consecutive year of growth. I would like to recognize our employees and supply chain partners around the world for their outstanding execution this year, which enabled us to maintain high levels of customer trust during an unprecedented industry ramp. As this is our year-end call, I'll begin with a brief review of our performance in 2026.

I'll provide our perspective on the market environment as demand continues to strengthen, Finally, I'll talk about how Applied has built the most enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing road map giving us a strong foundation for multiyear revenue and profit growth. In fiscal 2026, we grew revenue more than 21% and earnings nearly twice as fast, reflecting the operating leverage in our model. Based on the midpoint of our first quarter guidance, we expect our Semiconductor Systems revenue to be up more than 40% in calendar 2026.

As AI computing drives strong secular growth in semiconductors and wafer fab equipment, Applied is outgrowing the wafer fab equipment market because we've built leadership positions in the most enabling highest value technologies for AI computing. Our outperformance is driven by addressable market growth and nodal share gains in both advanced foundry-logic and DRAM, our strength in advanced packaging where we expect revenues to be up around 90% this calendar year, and our growing inspection and metrology business where we're on track to increase revenue more than 50% in calendar 2026. Demand for advanced semiconductors remains much higher than supply, and multiyear investments in new fab capacity are needed for the industry to close this supply-demand gap.

We expect 2027 to be another record year for the market and for Applied. Our current view is that wafer fab equipment demand will be up more than 30% year-over-year, and we are in a strong position to outperform the market again. The rate of industry growth will depend on how quickly the end-to-end semiconductor ecosystem can scale all the way from clean room construction to equipment components and raw material supply. At Applied, we're taking multiple actions to ensure we have the capacity and resources in place to support our customers' ramps. We are working more closely with customers on demand planning. Our largest customers are giving us rolling 8-quarter forecasts and earlier orders.

We're also deepening our collaboration with suppliers. In fact, I recently met with more than 250 senior executives from our key suppliers to align on capacity ramp expectations and readiness to serve a range of growth scenarios. In an AI data center, approximately 60% of the capital cost is silicon, and more than 85% of this silicon content is leading-edge foundry-logic, DRAM and advanced packaging. These 3 areas have the greatest impact on the AI computing road map, are expected to be the fastest-growing parts of wafer fab equipment in 2027 and together drive approximately 75% of WFE growth through 2030.

This is exactly where Applied has invested over the past several years to build the industry's most enabling portfolio, positioning us to outperform the market again in 2027 and beyond as we gained share at major device inflections. In mid-October, we unveiled the EPIC Center in Silicon Valley and hosted an investor breakfast in San Francisco. Thanks to all of you who attended in person or online. At the investor event, we shared 3 main themes: the unprecedented opportunities created by the AI era, the unique advantages in Applied's capabilities and portfolio to address these opportunities, and how we are creating more value for customers and capturing more value for Applied.

As the pace of the global AI deployment increases and the adoption of AI rapidly broadens, there is an intense battle for AI computing leadership that comes down to 2 interconnected races, and Applied is central to both. The first race is a race for technology leadership, which is enabled by accelerating the chip and packaging road maps that drive improvements in data center tokens per second per watt. The second is a race to add new chip manufacturing capacity by rapidly ramping new fabs while also optimizing the output and yield of existing factories. At Applied, we have created the industry's leading portfolio of materials innovation, integration innovation and yield innovation technologies.

The foundation for our leadership in materials innovation is our comprehensive and connected technology portfolio. We serve around 55% of total wafer fab equipment with #1 positions in CVD, PVD, epitaxy, CMP, implant, thermal processing, eBeam and conductor etch for advanced foundry-logic and DRAM. At advanced nodes, smaller feature sizes, 3-dimensional structures and the introduction of novel materials all drive immense process complexity. The interaction between process steps is critical, especially when it comes to engineering interfaces where the layers of materials are now just 1 to 2 nanometers thick.

That's why codeveloping deposition, etch, treatment, inspection and measurement technologies and solving integration challenges from the very start of development is such a powerful advantage and one that Applied is uniquely positioned to deliver. Applied has also built world-class integration, modeling and simulation teams as well as comprehensive lab infrastructure to accelerate transistor, wiring, memory and advanced packaging innovations. As yield and output become increasingly critical for customers, Applied is bringing new yield innovations to market.

We have the highest resolution and fastest eBeam imaging combined with industry-leading AI-enabled services that we call AIx. eBeam and AIx enable faster learning cycles in R&D, faster transfer and qualification of new technologies in pilot production, and more good chips out in high-volume manufacturing. Applied has by far the largest number of connected systems in the field with more than 37,000 chambers connected to AIx today, growing at more than 20% annually. Materials innovation, integration innovation and yield innovation are all accelerated by our EPIC platform.

EPIC enables Applied to develop technology side by side with customers and partners, providing them with much earlier access to next-generation Applied technology, accelerated cycles of learning, and faster transfer and ramp to high yield and output. For Applied, EPIC means we are designed in earlier at new chip and packaging architectures, gain better visibility into multiple generations of customer road maps and increase our R&D productivity. Since our last earnings call, we have added 4 more EPIC partners, Intel, KIOXIA, Besi and UCLA, bringing our total number of announced EPIC partnerships to 15, clear validation of the value of co-innovating with Applied.

At our investor event, we also outlined our 2025 to 2030 value creation targets to gain more than 2 points of wafer fab equipment share, increased service revenue per installed base tool by 20% or more and increased gross margin and operating margin by 5 and 10 points, respectively. I am confident we will make meaningful progress toward these targets in 2027, and all our teams are driving to higher targets. Before I hand over to Brice, I'll quickly summarize. Fiscal 2026 was a record year for Applied Materials, and we're on track to grow our Semiconductor Systems business more than 40% this calendar year.

We are growing faster than the wafer fab equipment market because of the strong leadership position we've built in leading-edge foundry-logic, DRAM and advanced packaging. These are the most enabling areas for AI computing, the fastest-growing parts of wafer fab equipment in 2027 and where Applied has invested strategically to build the industry's most enabling portfolio. We see 2027 as another record year for the industry and another year of outperformance for Applied, in which we expect to make significant progress towards our long-term targets. In short, AI is driving a multiyear expansion in semiconductor demand, and Applied has never been better positioned to lead and outgrow the market. Brice, over to you.

Brice Hill:Thanks, Gary. I'm pleased to share that Applied delivered a third consecutive quarter of double-digit sequential and year-over-year growth in revenue, operating profit and non-GAAP earnings per share. Fiscal Q4 also marks our 14th consecutive quarter of year-over-year gross margin expansion, which demonstrates the customer value of our highly enabling product and services portfolio. We expect to outperform the market this calendar year with strong growth in DRAM, leading-edge foundry-logic and advanced packaging, which is precisely where we've been investing to lead. I'd like to thank our manufacturing and operations teams and our partners for responding to further increases in customer demand and helping make these strong results possible.

On today's call, I'll update you on the demand environment, summarize our fiscal 2026 and Q4 results, and provide our Q1 business outlook. All the leading indicators we track continue to point upwards. Cloud CapEx is expected to increase more than 50% in 2027 to well over $1 trillion. AI token usage is growing exponentially. The increasing variety of AI models is enabling more applications and generating positive economics both for service providers and for early adopters like Applied Materials. AI is now a core part of everyday work at Applied. Over 80% of our employees use tools like Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic's Claude, along with newer domain-specific tools for materials discovery and engineering.

Inferencing is driving positive results throughout the company from equipment and software development to field service, operations and back office functions. All our software developers use AI, with an average productivity gain of over 40%. As a result, our monthly token consumption grew by more than 50x this year, and we expect our token and task usage to increase substantially in 2027, as we find more ways to use AI to accelerate revenue, improve customer service and operate more efficiently. AI continues to drive strong incremental growth in wafer demand with leading-edge logic and DRAM fabs running at full utilization. NAND is not far behind, and ICAPS is now in a healthy zone.

In the near term, a major focus is expanding our supply chain capacity to further increase the number of systems we can produce. We've raised our demand forecast to our suppliers every quarter this year, and they are partnering with us as the 2027 demand outlook continues to increase. We've mapped our supply chain, and our teams and partners are executing to manage pinch points and deliver another very strong growth year. Over the medium term, clean room capacity remains a gating factor for how much equipment the industry can consume. Fortunately, we're tracking more than 20 fab ramps and line expansions in 2027 alone.

We've created new teams and AIx technologies that will help our customers accelerate these ramps and maximize wafer output and yields. Longer term, demand signals from our customers remain very positive, with more than 10 major fabs and expansion projects added to our tracker for the third quarter in a row. Many of these new projects are not expected to come online until 2029 and 2030, which indicates a much higher level of demand across the 5- and 10-year horizon than previously planned in both logic and memory. At Applied, we're already working with customers to forecast their needs through 2030.

To support our customers' growth, we're investing to be able to double our systems output from Q4 '26 levels by 2028 and more than double our manufacturing and lab capacity by 2030. Next, I'll briefly summarize fiscal 2026 during which we grew revenue by over 21% to $34.4 billion, expanded non-GAAP gross margin by 130 basis points to 50.1% and increased non-GAAP EPS by 37% to $12.89. We generated double-digit revenue growth in Semi Systems and AGS and increased gross margins in both segments by around 150 basis points. Operating cash flow was $8.9 billion, up 11%. And after $2.7 billion in capital expenditures, free cash flow was $6.2 billion, up 9%.

We distributed over $4.7 billion to shareholders, including nearly $3.2 billion in stock buybacks and $1.6 billion in cash dividends. Turning to our Q4 results. We delivered the highest dollar growth in our history, generating record revenue of $10.4 billion, which is up 14% sequentially and 53% year-over-year. Non-GAAP gross margin increased to 50.6%, up 20 basis points sequentially and 250 basis points year-over-year, driven by favorable mix effects and higher pricing. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to a record 35.3%, up 130 basis points sequentially and 670 basis points year-over-year.

We delivered strong operating leverage with non-GAAP OpEx as a percent of revenue declining by 430 basis points year-over-year to 15.2%, and we increased non-GAAP earnings per share to a record $4.16, up 19% sequentially and 92% year-over-year. We plan to drive further gross margin expansion by introducing more enabling products and sharing in the value they create for our customers. We also plan to further increase operating leverage and margins as our AI and automation strategies enable us to scale our support function capabilities with minimal increases in headcount. Turning to segment performance in Q4. Semiconductor Systems delivered record revenue of $8 billion, up 14% sequentially and 64% year-over-year, including record sales in Korea and Taiwan.

DRAM grew strongly as we expected it would, and we posted record revenue in both DRAM and advanced packaging. From a product perspective in Q4, we had record revenue in deposition across PVD, CVD, ALD and epitaxy. We also had record revenue in etch, CMP and process control. Segment non-GAAP gross margin increased 240 basis points year-over-year to 55.2%, and non-GAAP operating margin increased over 940 basis points year-over-year to 39%. Applied Global Services delivered record revenue of $1.9 billion, up 26% year-over-year, reflecting record revenue in both services and spares. AGS gross margin grew 100 basis points year-over-year to 35.1%, and non-GAAP operating margin increased nearly 170 basis points to 30.5%.

Other revenue of $517 million was in line with our expectations for the quarter. We generated record operating cash flow of $3.3 billion in Q4. Capital expenditures declined sequentially to $684 million, resulting in record free cash flow of $2.6 billion. We distributed over $2.4 billion to shareholders, including $2 billion in stock buybacks and $421 million in cash dividends. We have $10.8 billion remaining in our share buyback authorization and continue to expect to distribute 80% to 100% of free cash flow to shareholders over time. Now I'll share our business outlook for Q1, which, as a reminder, is a 14-week quarter, which benefits AGS revenue growth in the period.

We expect company revenue of $11.1 billion, plus or minus $500 million, which is up 58% year-over-year at the midpoint. We expect non-GAAP EPS of $4.35, plus or minus $0.20, which is up 83% year-over-year. Within this outlook, we expect Semiconductor Systems revenue of around $8.7 billion, up 69% year-over-year; our first AGS quarter of $2 billion, up 28% year-over-year; and other revenue of around $400 million. We expect non-GAAP gross margin to increase to approximately 50.8%, up 170 basis points year-over-year, and we expect non-GAAP operating expenses of around $1.7 billion. We are modeling a non-GAAP tax rate of around 13%.

Finally, to help with your modeling after the 14-week quarter, we expect AGS revenue to remain close to Q1 levels in Q2 and OpEx in Q2 to be around 15% of revenue. In summary, AI continues to add a fast-growing and incremental layer of demand to the industry. The investments we've made to help enable this new wave have given us a rich and growing portfolio of highly enabling products and services. Our technology leadership in the most critical markets is now evident in our strong revenue growth and gross margin expansion.

Our focus on operating leverage is producing record operating margins and contributing to strong cash flow and shareholder distributions, including the largest quarterly share buyback in over 8 years. We continue to have long visibility from our customers, expect another strong record year in 2027 and are making substantial investments to be able to ramp to higher levels beyond next year. We have high confidence in our strategy and that we will demonstrate continuous progress on share gains, gross margin expansion and operating leverage. Now Mike, let's start the Q&A.

Michael Sullivan:Thanks, Brice.[Operator Instructions]Operator, let's please begin.

Operator:[Operator Instructions]. And our first question for today comes from the line of C.J. Muse from Cantor Fitzgerald.

Christopher Muse:I guess first question, would love to hear how the demand environment has changed or evolved in the last 3 months. You talked about visibility into '28, '29. Would love to hear more of how those conversations are going and if you can be kind of specific around end market, foundry-logic, DRAM, NAND. And I guess as part of it, I think, Brice, you talked about doubling your system output but also doubling manufacturing and lab capacity by 2030. If you can kind of bridge what kind of growth you're implying overall for shipments into the '28 and then '30 time frame as part of it would be very helpful.

Brice Hill:Sure. Nice to hear from you, C.J. So on the demand environment over the last 90 days, we've continued to see increases from customers. So we mentioned that we added more than 10 projects to our factory tracker. Those are fab -- new fab construction projects and existing fab conversions that are added, so that's the third quarter in a row that we've added more than 10 projects to the tracker. So the environment continues to strengthen. We see that the leading-edge logic and DRAM market are constrained, so customers are looking to add in -- add capacity as much as possible and pull in projects where they can do.

So the environment continues to be similar to prior quarters where it continues to strengthen from that perspective. And then on capacity investments, we are increasing our capacity. By 2028, we'll be able to double our output. So we just had an $8 billion quarter, so you can calculate that. That will be a capacity capability that we'll have. And then since we're not fully loaded today, doubling the output is one thing. Doubling our capacity is another thing, which we'll accomplish by 2030. So that will allow an even greater level of output.

The way we think of it is we have to have the capacity to cover all ranges of scenarios from an output perspective, and we're definitely looking at the growth rate that continues to pick up and making sure that we'll have the capacity to accomplish that. And then we're also sharing all this information with our suppliers.

Gary Dickerson:C.J., one thing I would add beyond the leading-edge foundry-logic and DRAM, which are being driven by AI, advanced packaging is another area that we see tremendous demand from customers. We talked about our business being up 90% in calendar year. We see very strong growth in '27 and also going forward in that segment also.

Christopher Muse:Very helpful. And a quick follow-up. If you could speak to kind of the work you're doing with your suppliers and your suppliers' suppliers, are you kind of funding, giving upfront deposits? I would love to hear kind of how you're facilitating what should be another tremendous kind of growth vector over the coming 2, 3 plus years?

Brice Hill:Yes, it's a great question, C.J. We talk about having over 2,000 suppliers and everybody needs to increase their output. And the first thing we've done is made sure we've got all of the data coming from our customers and getting to our suppliers. We talk about the 8-quarter forecast. We're getting that data to them. We're getting it in detail so that they can plan their output. The second thing that we're doing is working closely with the actual schedules for each quarter as we go through those 8 quarters of the year. And as far as investments, I think all the suppliers are incentivized to make these investments and grow their own profitability.

So we don't see any issues there. And from a -- what's it look like? We don't see any roadblocks to the higher levels of demand that are being envisioned. There will be plenty of pinch points that we talk about. So just about all the suppliers need to add capacity and add labor, so we're working on that with each of them.

Operator:And our next question comes from the line of Timothy Arcuri from UBS.

Timothy Arcuri:Brice, I'm wondering if you can give us just a sense of what the mix is assumed for fiscal Q1. And I ask because DRAM was up a ton for fiscal Q4, so I'm wondering if you think it will be up a lot again. Just if you can give us like a sense of what the mix looks like.

Brice Hill:Tim, yes, we're expecting similar trends looking at Q1, where DRAM and leading logic will be very strong. We think both of those end markets are constrained, so customers are doing whatever they can to increase capacity as rapidly as possible. So we actually see a similar mix to what we saw in Q4. And as we look through the year for '27, we expect that to stay about the same, so leading-edge DRAM and advanced packaging being the strongest growers for the year. And what's changing for us in '27 is that ICAPS, the mature logic technologies.

That looks like it will start to grow again and see greater investment in '27 as the market has digested the capacity and is getting normal from a capacity utilization perspective.

Gary Dickerson:Yes. Maybe one thing I would also add, Tim, is that relative to the ICAPS growth in '27, it's going to be growing much faster in non-China versus China.

Timothy Arcuri:Okay. Good. So Gary, I just wanted to ask, so the stock market sometimes leads fundamentals but not always. And we know that there is a mismatch between what the supply chain is building in terms of gigawatts that will be ready from a shell point of view versus what the chips are being built. So have you seen lately in the past, I don't know, few weeks or months or anything, have you seen any customers come to you and said, "Hey, seems great, but I might not want to take that tool exactly when I thought I would. And so maybe I want to take that a quarter or 2 or like a month or 2 later."?

Are you seeing any of that? Or is literally everyone pushing to get tools as fast as they can?

Gary Dickerson:No, very clear. The answer is no. Nobody is saying that they're not wanting the tools as fast as we can get them. I've been traveling quite a bit over the last couple of months, and we're constantly receiving requests from customers to accelerate our ramp and deliver earlier.

Operator:And our next question comes from the line of Vivek Arya from Bank of America Securities.

Vivek Arya:Gary, I wanted to ask the last question in a slightly different way, which is let's say, there are -- if there is any slowdown in data center build-out, right, whether it is next year and it impacts, whether it's next year or 2028, what do you think that does to WFE forecast? Do you think your customers are planning this deployment for the long term, so they're not going to be [ fazed ], right, by a slowdown, right, any short-term slowdown? Just how should investors think about the impact on the semicap industry if there is any temporary or a little bit extended slowdown in the build-out of data centers?

Gary Dickerson:Yes. Thanks for the question. So as I mentioned on the last question, what I'm seeing in some of our leading customer CEOs I'm meeting on a monthly basis is really requesting for us to ramp faster. I think demand in all of those areas, especially the ones that are being driven by AI, leading foundry-logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, demand is significant. And as you know, it takes time to ramp capacity. So I mean, you have to start with a view of computing demand and everything we see, everything I hear when I'm talking to companies through the ecosystem, computing demand is going to continue to go higher.

And so I don't see any signs from people that they're concerned about ramping too quickly. It's really the opposite where people want us to pull in and ramp faster. I don't know, Brice, if you want to add any color.

Brice Hill:Yes. I'll just add the point, Vivek, probably no surprise, but supply exceeds demand, especially DRAM and leading logic. So there's some buffer there between -- I'm sorry, sorry, demand exceeds supply. So there's some buffer there. And then we have markets that are underserved at this point also. So we have the PC market. You've got smartphone markets that are constrained, smart TVs that are constrained. So we think there's a considerable amount of buffer in the market even if data center were to have less demand over the next couple of years. And I think Gary highlighted, that's not what we're seeing, just to be clear.

Vivek Arya:All right. Very helpful. And for my follow-up, if I look at last year, when the year started, I think the expectation was that you would grow your Semi Systems over 20%, right? And now the actual number is likely to be closer to 40%, right? So you grew much faster. And there was the same conservatism around availability of clean room and so forth. So what got better through last year? And then I guess the real question is that when you were saying the industry will grow 30%, is that a line in the sand? Like, what can help the industry grow faster than 30%?

Like why can't the same thing that happened in '26 happen in '27 also?

Brice Hill:Yes, Vivek, great question. So we do think it's governed by clean room and clean room availability. Now to your point, all through last year, customers were able to either add clean room, pull in projects, work on projects that increased output from their factories by doing upgrades and those sorts of things. So those are the tools that customers have to increase output. I think the macro equation at the end of the day is guided by the clean room that can become available.

Operator:Our next question comes from the line of Stacy Rasgon from Bernstein Research.

Stacy Rasgon:First, so if you grew equipment, you're going to grow equipment more than 40% in '26. I guess what do you think WFE actually is growing on a percentage basis in 2026? And given you see WFE growing more than 30% in '27, do you think we should expect the same kind of outperformance in '27 relative to WFE that you're -- that we're seeing in '26?

Brice Hill:Stacy, yes, we do think that WFE -- that we're outperforming WFE in '26, and we expect that in '27 also, and that's on the strength of our top positions in leading logic, DRAM and advanced packaging and the strong mix to those being the fast-growing markets. So I think greater than 40% for our business and whatever our business is, slightly less than that for WFE for '26.

Stacy Rasgon:Got it. For my follow-up, you had some competitors calling out near-term supply constraints that actually impacted their outlook in the next quarter. Are you actually seeing any of it? It sounded like the same kind of stuff that you guys will be buying anyways. Are you seeing any of that? Is that actually -- I mean, as strong as the outlook is, is it impaired in any way by supply constraints? And would it be higher if you weren't seeing anything or if you're seeing anything at all?

Brice Hill:Yes, Stacy, good question. As I've highlighted, there's a few pinch points from a supply perspective. Our Q1 number would be slightly higher if everything were perfectly available. It's not a major impact, but we are working closely with all the suppliers. You saw 3 sequential quarters of more than double-digit growth as we went through the year. And supply chain is just reacting greatly. And we're working hard to increase the output, and we expect to increase the output every quarter this year.

Gary Dickerson:Yes, Stacy, I would add, at least for me, as I'm engaging with all of our customers, they want us to ship as fast as we can. I mean, just demand is very, very strong. Compute demand is very strong. So -- and as Brice said, I think our teams have done a really great job in ramping, but we have more work to do in '27. But we are in a very strong position to outperform going forward.

Operator:And our next question comes from the line of Atif Malik from Citi.

Atif Malik:I have a question on the DRAM road map. One of the memory makers is going to pursue 3D DRAM versus 4F2. And I know you guys have done a good job in the master classes covering the technology. If you can just remind us about Applied Materials' product positioning and opportunity on one versus another?

Gary Dickerson:Yes. Thanks for the question. One thing I would do is point to the investor breakfast, and there was a slide in there where we show the foundry-logic technology nodes and DRAM technology nodes. And what you see there in DRAM is, as you go to new versions of 6F2, we're gaining share. And then as you go to 4F2 and 3D DRAM, our servable market is increasing and our share is increasing multiple points. So from Applied Materials' standpoint, DRAM is a very strong segment for us. We're much larger than our nearest process equipment competitors. We're in very deep co-innovation relationships with every one of these different companies. So for Applied, we're in a good position.

Certainly, a 6F2 adoption continues, and you have new transistors for higher-speed bandwidth on those chips. And then as you go to 4F2 and 3D DRAM, we showed in that breakfast that our SAM share is increasing for 4F2 and 3D DRAM. We also show the SAM per 100,000 wafer starts increasing significantly as you go from 6F2 to 4F2 and then 3D DRAM. So again, from Applied's standpoint, we are deeply engaged with every one of these companies, and we have the most enabling technologies for these major inflections. So again, this is an area where we have very, very deep co-innovation relationships.

Atif Malik:And Brice, for the AGS part, you mentioned growing 20% annually and service revenue per tool also growing 20%. So how should we think about AGS growth for next year?

Brice Hill:Yes, we've highlighted mid-teens. So think 15% and -- for the horizon. The way I would think about that is the installed base grows 5% to 10% each year, and the revenue per tool grows 5% to 10% each year, so giving you a total of approximately 15%. This year, we grew faster on the -- benefiting from the increase in utilization across the whole ecosystem. So we're close to 100%. So you don't get that unique benefit again in the forward years. But those are the 2 building blocks, and we expect to continue to build new products that help the customers ramp and get the highest yields.

Operator:And our next question comes from the line of Krish Sankar from TD Cowen.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan:Brice, I just want to follow up on the component supply question. It seems like you're not adding inventory as much and days of inventories was also down 10 days. I'm wondering why wouldn't you be more aggressive in adding inventory. And along the same path, you kind of gave some color on AGS in April. Any idea to think about Semi Systems in April quarter? And then I had a quick follow-up.

Brice Hill:Yes. Thanks, Krish. Nice to hear from you. So we added just over $300 million of inventory in the quarter, $6.9 billion of inventory. And I think it's fair. I would like to have even more inventory, so we're working on that with the suppliers. And I'll just highlight again, we had 3 quarters of double-digit increases in output. So we're definitely pushing the system and we'll continue working on that as we go through the year. And it's a good point. We would like to have more inventory.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan:And any color on April quarter Semi Systems?

Brice Hill:Yes. Nothing specific at this point. Yes, what we said was we expect to increase output every quarter this year as we work with the supply chain.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan:Got you. And as a quick follow-up, Gary, this year, it seems like when you started the year to ending the year, DRAM WFE actually grew pretty substantially. A lot of it is conversion-driven. How to think about it in '27? Do you think conversions slow down and greenfield picks up? Or do you think conversions continue for next year?

Gary Dickerson:I think our customers are doing everything they can to increase output, everything they can do on upgrades and certainly much more aggressive investments in greenfield. So I would say both. One thing that I've seen more so than any point in my career is the focus on yield and output innovation. We talked about this in the investor breakfast. Every customer that I'm talking to, they want more good chips per wafer, and they want more wafers out. So I would say that -- and again, these -- I traveled quite a bit over the last couple of months with all of our leading customers. This is creating tremendous pull for our AGS business.

We talked about having over 37,000 chambers connected to these AI-enabled AIx servers.
